cases.title: Bastion security group opened to 0.0.0.0/0 on SSH
cases.why: The most common real incident. Someone is locked out, widens the rule to unblock themselves, and the temporary fix is never reverted.

cases.title: New security group allowing every protocol on every port from anywhere
cases.why: Written during an outage to rule out the network as a cause, then left in place because the outage had a different root cause and nobody revisited it.

cases.title: PostgreSQL exposed to the internet through aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule
cases.why: The newer singular rule resource uses different attribute names (cidr_ipv4, ip_protocol). Scanners written against the inline block shape read it as having no rules at all and report nothing.

cases.title: MySQL source range widened from a /24 to a /8
cases.why: The diff shows one string changing and still contains a CIDR, so it reads as scoped. It admits sixteen million more addresses than it did.

cases.title: S3 block_public_policy turned off
cases.why: Disabling the guard exposes nothing by itself, which is exactly why it gets approved. The bucket policy that makes it matter arrives in a later change.

cases.title: Production database given a public endpoint
cases.why: Usually done to let a BI tool or a contractor connect without setting up peering. The security group becomes the only remaining control.

cases.title: Internal load balancer flipped to internet-facing
cases.why: A one-character diff, false to true, that changes the reachability of every target behind the load balancer, including targets added later by other teams.

cases.title: Network ACL entry allowing 0.0.0.0/0 into a private subnet
cases.why: The network ACL is the subnet's independent boundary and the only control still standing when a security group is wrong. An allow-all entry removes the second layer while the first still looks correct.

cases.title: Unrestricted egress added to a workload security group
cases.why: Copied from the provider documentation's example block, which uses 0.0.0.0/0 on protocol -1. It is the path data leaves by.

cases.title: EKS control plane endpoint made public with no allow-list
cases.why: Enabled to make kubectl work from a laptop. The Kubernetes API is then internet-reachable with IAM as the only barrier.

cases.title: Subnet switched to auto-assign public IPs
cases.why: Changes the character of every instance launched into the subnet from then on, including instances created by autoscaling long after this review.

cases.title: Security group whose rules are computed at apply time
cases.why: The rules come from a module output that Terraform cannot resolve during plan. A reviewer sees an empty ingress list and approves it. The tool has to say it cannot review this rather than say it found nothing.

cases.title: Application port 8080 opened directly to the internet
cases.why: Added to debug a load balancer health check. It routes around the load balancer, and with it TLS termination, the WAF and the access logs. The port is not a database port, so a rule that only knows about well-known services says nothing at all.

cases.title: Production database destroyed because its block was deleted
cases.why: A module refactor removes a resource block. Terraform renders one line with a minus sign, and the data is not in version control.

cases.title: Database replaced because an immutable attribute changed
cases.why: Changing the subnet group forces recreation. Terraform shows -/+ and the reviewer reads it as an update. The new instance comes up empty.

cases.title: NAT gateway replaced destroy-first, cutting egress for the subnet
cases.why: Without create_before_destroy there is a window with no NAT gateway. Every instance in the private subnet loses outbound connectivity for the duration.

cases.title: Deletion protection disabled and final snapshot skipped in one change
cases.why: Neither attribute changes anything on apply. Together they remove both controls that would have stopped, or made recoverable, the next destroy.

cases.title: Plan computed against a state that no longer matches reality
cases.why: Someone changed the security group in the console. Every diff in this plan is a diff against a picture that is already wrong, and applying it silently reverts their change.

cases.title: Sensitive value changes with the diff redacted
cases.why: Terraform prints (sensitive value) on both sides. The change is real, unreviewable from the plan, and anything still holding the old value breaks at apply.

cases.title: A security group change that also rewrites an IAM role
cases.why: The pull request says it adjusts a security group. The plan also modifies an IAM role, which is the kind of thing that gets approved by association with the change that was actually reviewed.

cases.title: Bucket policy that Terraform cannot resolve before apply
cases.why: The policy is rendered from a data source that resolves at apply time. Approving the plan approves a policy document nobody has read.

cases.title: KMS key destroyed while data encrypted under it remains
cases.why: Deleting the key is a single line. Everything encrypted with it becomes permanently unreadable, including backups taken before the change.

cases.title: CloudWatch log group replaced, discarding retained events
cases.why: Renaming a log group replaces it. The retained events go with the old one, which matters most in exactly the situation you need them for.

cases.title: Every port opened to 0.0.0.0/1 and 128.0.0.0/1
cases.why: The two halves are the whole internet. Both read as ordinary scoped CIDRs in a diff, and every check that tests a block for /0 lets them through. This is the cheapest way to defeat a scanner, and it needs no privileges to write.

cases.title: The VPC default security group opened to everything
cases.why: aws_default_security_group applies to every network interface with no explicit group, so it has the widest reach available. It is a different resource type from aws_security_group, which is enough for a type-keyed checker to miss it.

cases.title: The account-level S3 public access block deleted
cases.why: Same four guards as the per-bucket resource, applied to every bucket in the account at once. Removing it is strictly worse than the per-bucket case, and it is a different resource type.

cases.title: A private route table gains a default route to an internet gateway
cases.why: No security group changes and no public IP attribute flips. The subnets on this table simply become routable from the internet. This is the step that makes an address reachable, and reviews almost never look at route tables.

cases.title: A workload subnet re-associated with a route table that reaches the internet
cases.why: The subnet does not change. Its security groups do not change. One association points somewhere else and every instance in it is now publicly routable.

cases.title: Database rule sourced from a security group, which is open to the world
cases.why: Referencing a group instead of a CIDR is the advice everyone gives, and it is only a restriction if the referenced group is one. Here the group admits the whole internet, so the database does too. Nothing in this rule says so.

cases.title: A VPC peering connection and a /16 route across it
cases.why: Segmentation is what limits how far an intrusion travels. A peering connection with a route wide enough to cover the peer's whole network is a flat network with extra steps, and it affects every workload on both sides.

cases.title: The deny entry that was the subnet's boundary is deleted
cases.why: Removing a deny is the same harm as adding an allow, expressed as a deletion. After the change there is nothing in the end state to object to, so a check that reads the planned state rather than the change sees a clean result.

cases.title: A bucket policy statement granting Principal "*"
cases.why: The public access block is the guard; the policy is the thing the guard exists to stop. A bucket with a wildcard policy is world-readable, and the resource that says so is a JSON string inside an attribute.

cases.title: A shared prefix list gains 0.0.0.0/0
cases.why: No security group appears in this plan. Every rule in the account that references the list widens at once, which is the largest change-to-blast-radius ratio available in a single line.

cases.title: A world-open rule whose port range is computed at apply time
cases.why: The ports come from a variable Terraform cannot resolve. A checker that treats an empty port range as 'no ports' concludes there is nothing sensitive behind it and reports the most alarming case as the least.

cases.title: A Redshift cluster given a public endpoint
cases.why: publicly_accessible is not an RDS-only attribute, and on Redshift it defaults to true, so a cluster created without mentioning it is public. The warehouse usually holds more than any single application database.

cases.title: A launch template starts assigning public IP addresses
cases.why: The attribute is inside a nested network_interfaces block, and it applies to every instance the autoscaling group creates from now on, long after this review is forgotten.

cases.title: The account's CloudTrail trail is destroyed
cases.why: Nothing else in the plan has to be wrong for this to matter: it removes the ability to find out later what any of the rest of it did. After the apply there is no trail resource left for an end-state check to have an opinion on.

cases.title: Automated backups disabled on a production database
cases.why: Setting backup_retention_period to zero does not only stop future backups, it deletes the ones already taken. Applying it changes nothing you can see; it changes what is possible after the next mistake.

cases.title: A policy statement granting every action on every resource
cases.why: It arrives as one extra statement in a policy that was already there, usually while unblocking a deployment. The change is AdministratorAccess by another name, and the diff is four lines of JSON inside a string.

cases.title: iam:PassRole granted on every role, paired with ec2:RunInstances
cases.why: Neither permission reads as administrator access. Together they let the holder start an instance carrying any role in the account, including roles far more privileged than the one doing the passing.

cases.title: A role's trust policy changed to accept any principal
cases.why: The role's own permissions do not change at all, so a permissions review finds nothing. What changed is who is allowed to become it, which is the other half of the question and lives in a different attribute.

cases.title: iam:CreatePolicyVersion granted to a build role
cases.why: It is a single IAM action on a policy the role already manages, and it reads as housekeeping. It lets the holder write a new default version of any policy, granting itself anything.

cases.title: The MFA condition removed from an existing Allow statement
cases.why: The statement grants the same actions on the same resources before and after. Only the condition is gone. Nothing about the resulting policy records that a guard rail was ever there, so a check on the end state cannot see it.

cases.title: An Allow statement using NotAction
cases.why: Allow with NotAction grants everything except a list, which means it grants every service AWS launches from now on, in advance. It is almost always meant to be a Deny, and it reads as a tight policy.

cases.title: AdministratorAccess attached to a service role
cases.why: A managed policy attachment is one line in a plan and is approved as boilerplate. This one grants the account.

cases.title: An IAM policy rendered from a value Terraform cannot resolve
cases.why: Approving the plan approves a set of permissions nobody has read. Reporting nothing here is indistinguishable from reporting that the policy is fine.

cases.title: A public web server serving 443 to the internet
cases.why: This is what a correct public service looks like. A tool that calls this critical is a tool people turn off.

cases.title: A tag change on a security group that was already open to the world
cases.why: The single most important negative control. The exposure is real but it is not this change's doing. A tool that blocks this pull request is blocking the wrong pull request, and teaches the team that its findings are noise.

cases.title: An SSH rule narrowed from the internet to the VPN range
cases.why: A strict improvement. Reporting it would mean the tool cannot tell the direction of a change, only that one happened.

cases.title: A launch template replaced, which loses nothing
cases.why: Replacement is only alarming when something irreplaceable goes with it. Treating every -/+ as critical is how a tool becomes background noise.

cases.title: A policy whose wildcard is replaced with specific actions
cases.why: A strict improvement. A tool that reports this cannot tell the direction of a change, only that one happened, and the team learns to ignore it.

cases.title: A cross-account trust policy naming one role, with an ExternalId
cases.why: This is what a correct cross-account grant looks like. Reporting it would make every legitimate integration a finding.

cases.title: A private subnet's default route pointing at a NAT gateway
cases.why: This is how a private subnet is supposed to reach out. It is a default route, so a rule keyed on 0.0.0.0/0 alone would report it; the target is what matters.

cases.title: A network ACL allow entry scoped to the VPC range
cases.why: Allow entries are normal; the question is what they admit. Reporting every allow would make the rule useless on any real network ACL.
